ra: The Mujaddidi is the early-modern revivalist sub-branch of the Naqshbandiyya, receiving and renewing its silsila and silent-dhikr method.
Doctrinally and organizationally continuous with the parent Naqshbandi order.
Sirhindi is the eponymous founder-figure (Mujaddid) of the Naqshbandi-Mujaddidi branch.
Initiated into the Naqshbandi order (via Baqi Billah) before reforming it into the Mujaddidi line.
Sirhindi's wahdat al-shuhud was developed in critical reception of Ibn Arabi's wahdat al-wujud, engaging the Akbari metaphysics directly.
Al-Nabulsi was the foremost early-modern Akbari commentator, defending and expounding Ibn Arabi's wahdat al-wujud.
Al-Nabulsi held Naqshbandi (and Qadiri) affiliation alongside his Akbari commitments.
Shah Waliullah was initiated in the Naqshbandi-Mujaddidi line and worked to harmonize its shuhudi reform with Akbari wujudi metaphysics.
His Hujjat Allah al-Baligha and related works engaged Ibn Arabi's metaphysics, seeking to reconcile wahdat al-wujud with Sirhindi's wahdat al-shuhud.
The Tijaniyya is a tariqa (Sufi path), instantiating the general category of the Sufi order.
Ahmad al-Tijani is the eponymous founder and supreme master of the Tijaniyya.
Ali Harazim was Tijani's foremost disciple and compiler of the order's foundational text.
Harazim received the teaching directly from Ahmad al-Tijani, recording it in the Jawahir al-Ma'ani.
The Darqawiyya is a Shadhili-derived tariqa, instantiating the Sufi-order category.
Mawlay al-Arabi al-Darqawi is the eponymous founder of the Darqawiyya.
The Khalwatiyya is a major tariqa, instantiating the Sufi-order category.
Niyazi Misri founded the Misriyya branch of the Khalwatiyya.
Mustafa al-Bakri was the great early-modern reviver and master of the Khalwatiyya.
Bursevi's tafsir Ruh al-Bayan draws heavily on Akbari metaphysics, transmitting Ibn Arabi's teaching.
Bursevi's exegesis incorporates Rumi's mystical poetry and themes.
Al-Sha'rani transmitted and defended Ibn Arabi (notably an abridged Futuhat), while harmonizing law and Sufism.
Al-Sha'rani was a Shadhili master who founded an Egyptian Shadhili sub-line (Sha'rawiyya).
Uthman dan Fodio was a Qadiri shaykh who venerated Abd al-Qadir al-Jilani and propagated the Qadiri order in West Africa.
Bulleh Shah belonged to the Qadiri-Shattari stream (via Inayat Shah Qadiri), in the Qadiri lineage descending from al-Jilani.
Sultan Bahu founded the Sarwari Qadiri sub-line, a branch of the Qadiri order of al-Jilani.
Shah Abdul Latif Bhittai's Risalo is steeped in the love-mysticism tradition of Rumi (whose Mathnawi he is said to have carried and recited), reworking it into Sindhi idiom.
Bhittai stood in the Sindhi Qadiri devotional milieu descending from al-Jilani.
Abd al-Qadir al-Jaza'iri edited and championed Ibn Arabi's al-Futuhat al-Makkiyya and built his Mawaqif on Akbari metaphysics.
He was a Qadiri amir-saint in the lineage of Abd al-Qadir al-Jilani (his namesake).
Khalid al-Baghdadi was a Mujaddidi master who founded the Khalidi sub-branch within that line.
The Khalidi line is a renewal current within the broader Naqshbandi order.
Khwaja Mir Dard was a Naqshbandi-Mujaddidi shaykh who developed the Tariqa Muhammadiyya Khalisa within that branch.
Dara Shikoh's comparative mysticism (Majma al-Bahrayn) was steeped in Akbari wahdat al-wujud.
Dara Shikoh was initiated in the Qadiri order (via Mulla Shah Badakhshi and Mian Mir), in al-Jilani's lineage.
